en: “Where are you from?” “I am from Rome.”
explain: _unde?_ asks “from where?”. For the name of a town, Latin uses the ablative with no preposition: _Rōmā sum_ = I am from Rome.
distractors: “From” a town is the ablative: _Rōmā_, not the accusative _Rōmam_.

en: “Where are you from?” “I am from America.”
modernNote: America was unknown to the Romans, so this is a modern name with Latin endings.
explain: A country needs _ex_ (“out of”) plus the ablative: _ex Americā_. America is a modern name, so a Roman would not have known it.
distractors: _in Americā_ means “in America”. “From America” is _ex Americā_.

en: “Where do you live?” “I live in Rome.”
explain: _ubi?_ asks “where?”. For a town, _Rōmae_ means “at Rome” (a special form called the locative). _habitō_ is “I live”.
distractors: Town names need no _in_: _Rōmae_ alone means “at Rome”.

en: “How old are you?” “I am twenty years old.”
explain: Romans said “born of twenty years”: _vīgintī annōs nātus sum_. The years are accusative plural (_annōs_), and _nātus_ means “born”.
distractors: The years are the object here: accusative _annōs_.

explain: _quid facis?_ = what are you doing? The _-s_ is “you”, so the answer ends in _-ō_: _labōrō_ (I work).

en: “Do you have a brother?” “Yes, I have a brother.”
explain: _-ne_ makes a yes/no question. _frātrem_ is the accusative singular, the thing you have.
distractors: _frāter_ is nominative. What you have is accusative: _frātrem_.
_minimē_ means “no”. The answer here is yes: _etiam_.

en: “Do you have a sister?” “No, I do not have a sister.”
tag: no, I do not have a sister
explain: _minimē_ means “no” (literally “least of all”), and _nōn_ goes before the verb to negate it.
distractors: Without _nōn_ this says “I do have a sister”.
_soror_ is nominative. What you do not have is accusative: _sorōrem_.

en: I don't understand. Say it again, please.
explain: _nōn_ negates the verb: _nōn intellegō_ = I do not understand. Then ask for a repeat with the command _dīc_ (no final -e) and _iterum_ (again). This is the most useful pair of sentences for a learner.
distractors: _dīcite_ is to several people. To one person: _dīc_.

explain: _dīc_ is the irregular command to one person (no final -e), and _iterum_ means “again”. _quaesō_ adds “please”.
distractors: _dīcite_ is to several people. To one person: _dīc_.
_dīcit_ is “he says”. A command to one person is _dīc_.

explain: _dīc_ is the command to one person and _lentē_ is an adverb (“slowly”), which never changes. A learner's other useful sentence.
distractors: _dīcite_ is to several people. To one person: _dīc_.

explain: _-ne_ makes a question, and the answer turns _intellegis_ (you) into _intellegō_ (I).
distractors: _minimē_ means “no”. The answer here is yes: _etiam_.

explain: _hoc_ means “this”. After _est_ the noun that says what it is stays nominative: _liber_ (not _librum_).
distractors: After _est_ the noun is nominative: _liber_, not the accusative _librum_.
_hoc_ is singular, so the verb is _est_.
_librī_ is genitive or plural. “A book” is nominative singular: _liber_.

explain: _occupātus_ (busy) and _ōtiōsus_ (free, at leisure) are adjectives that agree with the speaker. A man says _ōtiōsus_; a woman says _ōtiōsa_. The Romans valued _ōtium_ (leisure), the opposite of _negōtium_ (business).
distractors: _ōtiōsa_ is feminine. A man says _ōtiōsus_ (this course assumes you are a man; a woman would say _ōtiōsa_).

en: “Where are you going?” “I am going to the forum.”
explain: _quō?_ asks “where to?”. _ad forum_ takes the accusative, and _eō_ is “I go”.
_sciō_ means “I know”. _paulum_ is “a little”, and _Latīnē_ is an adverb: “in Latin”, so it never changes.

en: “What are you learning?” “I am learning the Latin language.”
explain: _lingua_ is feminine, so its adjective is _Latīna_, and as the object of _discō_ both are accusative: _linguam Latīnam_.
distractors: _lingua_ is feminine, so the adjective is _Latīnam_.
